title: Apron Feeder

introduction.definition: An apron feeder is a heavy-duty feeder that draws material out from under a hopper or bin. Overlapping steel pans are bolted to two strands of crawler-type chain. The chains run around a head (drive) sprocket and a tail sprocket. The pans carry the material forward at low speed and drop it off the head end. It is built to take large lumps and the impact of material dumped from trucks.
applications: Primary feeding of run-of-mine ore from a dump hopper to a primary crusher
Withdrawing coal, limestone and ore from stockpile tunnels
Feeding sticky or wet material that would hang on a vibrating feeder
key_points: Handles large lumps and high impact
Low speed — feed rate set by bed depth × width × speed
Variable-speed drive controls the feed rate
Pans and chains are the main wear items
introduction.summary: An apron feeder pulls heavy, lumpy ore out from under a hopper at a controlled rate. Overlapping steel pans bolted to crawler-type chains form a moving floor; the drive sprockets at the head pull the chain, and the pans dump the ore over the head. It withstands impact from large lumps and high loads.

selection_notes: Size the width for about 2–3 × the maximum lump size and the bed depth for the required rate at a moderate speed.
Check the hopper load on the pans (draw-down vs static load) — it sets drive power.

foundation: Support on steelwork or a concrete plinth designed for the hopper/bin load on the feeder plus impact and dynamic loads.
Isolate vibrating machines from the structure with their springs/rubber mounts — never weld or rigidly bolt the vibrating body to the structure.
alignment: Set the feeder at the designed slope and centre it under the hopper outlet; set skirt boards and the hopper gate to the design bed depth.
Align drive and driven shafts (laser or dial gauge) or set the exciter motors as the maker specifies.
piping: Chutes and skirts: allow a gap that widens in the direction of travel so material does not jam; fit dust seals and connect dust extraction where required.
Leave clear access for liner change and for the hopper shut-off gate.
commissioning: Run empty first: check direction, amplitude/speed, temperatures and noise.
Load gradually, check the material bed is even and the discharge rate matches the set-point; record motor current as a baseline.

routine.task: Check for spillage, pan damage and chain tracking.
Check drive temperature and oil level.

periodic.task: Measure chain/roller wear and pan gaps; adjust chain tension at the tail.
Inspect skirt liners and hopper wear liners.

overhaul.task: Replace worn pans, chain links, rollers and sprockets as a set where pitch has grown.

lubrication: Gear reducer: oil to grade and change interval.
Chain rollers and shaft bearings: grease to schedule (sealed-for-life rollers need none).

causes: Large lumps dropped from height without a rock box
remedies: Keep a material cushion in the hopper

symptoms: Material on the floor under the feeder
causes: Bed depth too high for the skirts
Packed material, frozen or sticky feed
remedies: Clear build-up; reduce bed depth; check VSD settings

safety: Lock out and block the pans before working under a loaded hopper — stored material can drive the pans.
Never clear blockages with the feeder running.

script.narration: This module introduces the Apron Feeder.
An apron feeder is a heavy-duty feeder that draws material out from under a hopper or bin.
Overlapping steel pans are bolted to two strands of crawler-type chain.
The chains run around a head (drive) sprocket and a tail sprocket.

Typical applications include primary feeding of run-of-mine ore from a dump hopper to a primary crusher; withdrawing coal, limestone and ore from stockpile tunnels; feeding sticky or wet material that would hang on a vibrating feeder; reclaim from large bins.

script.narration: How the Apron Feeder works.
Material from the hopper sits on the overlapping pans.
The drive turns the head sprocket and shaft, pulling the chain and pans forward.
The pans carry a bed of material under the hopper skirts at low speed.
At the head end material falls off into the crusher or chute; the empty pans return underneath around the tail sprocket.
The flow overlay traces the liquid from suction to discharge.

video_tutorials.title: Apron Feeder — Maintenance

script.narration: Maintenance essentials for the Apron Feeder.
Check for spillage, pan damage and chain tracking.
Check drive temperature and oil level.
Measure chain/roller wear and pan gaps; adjust chain tension at the tail.
Inspect skirt liners and hopper wear liners.
Replace worn pans, chain links, rollers and sprockets as a set where pitch has grown.
Watch for chain or pan breakage: sudden stop, broken pans, spillage. Common cause: large lumps dropped from height without a rock box.
Watch for excessive spillage: material on the floor under the feeder. Common cause: skirt gap or liners worn.
Watch for drive overload: high current, trips. Common cause: packed material, frozen or sticky feed.
Record every inspection so trends — vibration, temperature, leakage and performance — can be compared over time.
